Chapter 2: The Weight of Oppression—How Colonialism Shapes the Mind
Living under colonial rule doesn't just change the world around you—it quietly seeps into your mind, shaping the way you think about yourself, and even those closest to you.
At first, the effects are so subtle, you might not even notice. But over time, it's like a shadow stretching across everything. People begin to see themselves through the eyes of those in power, and that can leave scars that run deep.
Imagine a young student, excited to learn, but slowly starting to doubt herself. Maybe her teachers dismiss her accent, or make fun of her family's traditions. Eventually, she starts to think that to succeed, she has to be more like the colonizer—maybe speak a different language, dress a certain way, or even change her name. The message she gets, over and over, is that to be valued, she has to leave her old self behind.
This way of thinking spreads quickly. In families, parents start to worry that their kids won’t have a future unless they fit in with the dominant culture. Friends might tease each other for holding on to “old-fashioned” ways. Even holidays and rituals that once meant everything start to lose their meaning, replaced by customs and celebrations from somewhere else.
The colonizer’s power isn’t just enforced by laws or force—it’s woven right into daily life. Think about the ads you see, the textbooks you read, even the movies everyone talks about. All those things send the same message: that the colonized are somehow less—less smart, less capable, less worthy. And after hearing that long enough, a lot of people start to believe it.
Sometimes, that pain and frustration turn inward. People get angry at themselves, or even at their own communities. Instead of blaming the system that created these struggles, they end up blaming each other.
But colonialism leaves its mark on everyone. The colonizers themselves are changed by the system they uphold. They learn to see themselves as superior, to justify their privileges, and to look away from the suffering around them. It's a cycle that dehumanizes everyone, making real connection and understanding almost impossible.
Still, there are quiet moments when the truth slips through. Maybe it’s a parent watching their child struggle with shame—feeling a sharp mix of guilt and anger. Or an elder remembering stories of resistance and pride, and wondering what it would take to bring that spirit back.
The psychological scars of colonialism run deep, but they're not permanent. Healing begins when people start to question the stories they've been told—when they remember that their history is rich, their culture matters, and their voices are powerful.
You know, it’s not easy. Sometimes, it’s even painful. But that slow process of remembering and reclaiming—that’s the first step toward real dignity and hope.
